questions.stem: About the organisation of the vascular system:

options.label: A
options.text: There are three circulations: pulmonary, systemic (caval) and portal

options.label: B
options.text: Blood leaving the heart passes through arteries, arterioles, then capillaries

options.label: C
options.text: The tunica intima consists of endothelium and an elastic lamina in connective tissue

options.label: D
options.text: The tunica media is composed mainly of collagen

options.label: E
options.text: The endothelium is simple squamous epithelium lining all vessels

questions.why: False: D. Mainly SMOOTH MUSCLE.

questions.stem: Arteries:

options.label: A
options.text: The aorta is an elastic artery whose recoil maintains flow in diastole

options.label: B
options.text: Smaller arteries and arterioles have a thicker smooth muscle layer

options.label: C
options.text: The labial anastomosis between the two facial arteries is an actual anastomosis

options.label: D
options.text: Coronary artery anastomoses are actual, freely compensating channels

options.label: E
options.text: In some tissues arterioles empty into venules through arteriovenous shunts

questions.why: False: D. They are POTENTIAL anastomoses.

questions.stem: Blood flow through a single capillary bed is regulated mainly by:

options.label: B
options.text: the tunica adventitia of the venule

options.label: C
options.text: the valves of the small veins

options.label: D
options.text: the elastic lamina of the arteriole

questions.why: Organ flow is set by precapillary sphincters together with the resistance of the muscular small arteries.

questions.stem: Capillaries:

options.label: A
options.text: are the narrowest vessels, about 7–10 µm across

options.label: B
options.text: are the functional exchange unit of the circulation

options.label: C
options.text: have smooth muscle and connective tissue layers in their wall

options.label: D
options.text: of the CNS lack intercellular channels, contributing to the blood–brain barrier

options.label: E
options.text: are wide enough for the red cell, which is about 6–8 µm

notes.C: Only a single layer of endothelium.

questions.why: False: C. Only a single layer of endothelium.

questions.stem: Sinusoidal (discontinuous) capillaries are found in all of the following EXCEPT the:
questions.why: The kidney has fenestrated capillaries.

questions.stem: Veins:

options.label: A
options.text: have thinner walls and wider lumens than the companion arteries

options.label: B
options.text: have three coats but no elastic lamina

options.label: C
options.text: in the limbs are doubled as superficial veins and venae comitantes

options.label: D
options.text: of the limbs and neck commonly have valves that prevent reflux

options.label: E
options.text: have a thicker tunica media than arteries of the same size

notes.E: MUCH LESS muscle in the media.

questions.why: False: E. MUCH LESS muscle in the media.

questions.stem: In pulmonary artery catheterisation, the catheter passes in order through the:

options.label: A
options.text: femoral artery, aorta, left ventricle, then the pulmonary trunk

options.label: B
options.text: subclavian vein, left atrium, mitral valve, pulmonary trunk

options.label: C
options.text: internal jugular, right atrium, tricuspid valve, pulmonary trunk

options.label: D
options.text: internal jugular vein, right ventricle, mitral valve, aorta

options.label: E
options.text: external jugular vein, coronary sinus, right ventricle, aorta

questions.why: A flow-guided (Swan-Ganz) catheter follows venous return: internal jugular vein, right atrium, through the tricuspid valve and right ventricle, into the pulmonary trunk; it never enters the arterial/left side.

notes.B: Arterial route to the left heart.
notes.D: Mitral valve and aorta are left-sided.

questions.stem: Which is an unpaired (visceral) branch of the thoracic aorta?
questions.why: Unpaired: bronchial, pericardial, oesophageal, mediastinal.

questions.stem: The superior mesenteric artery arises from the aorta at the:
questions.why: The superior mesenteric artery leaves the aorta at the lower border of L1, just below the coeliac trunk (T12); the inferior mesenteric arises lower, at L3.

questions.stem: The splenic artery is a branch of the:
questions.why: The coeliac trunk gives left gastric, splenic and common hepatic arteries.

questions.stem: The vessel that crosses in front of the aorta, just below the origin of the SMA, is the:
questions.why: The left renal vein crosses anterior to the aorta; the right renal artery passes behind the IVC.

notes.C: Drains into the left renal vein.
notes.E: Lies behind the pancreas higher up.

questions.stem: The elastic recoil that keeps blood flowing in diastole is a property mainly of the:
questions.why: Their thick elastic laminae stretch in systole and recoil in diastole.

questions.stem: An example of an actual (true) arterial anastomosis is between the:

options.label: B
options.text: segmental branches of the renal artery

options.label: C
options.text: segmental branches of the splenic artery

options.label: D
options.text: labial branches of the facial arteries

questions.why: The labial arteries join freely across the midline.

questions.stem: Sudden blockage of a coronary artery often causes infarction because its anastomoses are:
questions.why: They can enlarge with gradual narrowing, but not quickly.

questions.stem: The aortic sinuses (of Valsalva) give origin to the:
questions.why: The first part of the ascending aorta.

questions.stem: The ascending aorta begins at the level of the:
questions.why: It ends at the right 2nd costal cartilage, where the arch begins.

questions.stem: The arch of the aorta ends at the:

options.label: A
options.text: right side of the body of T2

options.label: C
options.text: left side of the body of T4

questions.why: Level with the sternal angle; it continues as the descending aorta.

questions.stem: The baroreceptors of the aortic arch lie in its:
questions.why: They sense stretch of the wall.

questions.stem: The ligamentum arteriosum connects the arch of the aorta to the:
questions.why: Remnant of the ductus arteriosus; the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks below it.

notes.B: Passes under the arch to the right.

questions.stem: Which pulmonary artery is longer and wider?

options.label: A
options.text: Right, passing under the aortic arch

options.label: B
options.text: Left, passing under the aortic arch

options.label: C
options.text: Right, passing in front of the SVC

questions.why: It passes behind the ascending aorta and SVC to the right lung.

questions.stem: The posterior intercostal arteries from the thoracic aorta supply which spaces?
questions.why: The first two come from the superior intercostal artery; T12 is subcostal.

notes.B: 1st and 2nd come from the costocervical trunk.

questions.stem: The aorta enters the abdomen at the level of:
questions.why: Behind the median arcuate ligament.

questions.stem: The abdominal aorta divides into the common iliac arteries at the level of:

options.label: C
options.text: S1, at the sacral promontory level

options.label: D
options.text: L4, slightly left of the midline

questions.why: The bifurcation lies just to the left of the midline.

questions.stem: Which artery supplies the pelvic viscera?
questions.why: The common iliac has no branches until it divides.

questions.stem: The middle colic artery is a branch of the:
questions.why: SMA branches: ileocolic, right colic and middle colic.

questions.stem: The superior rectal artery is the continuation of the:
questions.why: IMA: left colic, sigmoid, then superior rectal.

questions.stem: The arterial supply of the gut changes from the SMA to the IMA at the:

options.label: A
options.text: ileocaecal junction of the right colon

options.label: B
options.text: hepatic flexure of the ascending colon

options.label: C
options.text: distal third of the transverse colon

options.label: D
options.text: junction of descending and sigmoid colon

options.label: E
options.text: duodenojejunal flexure of the small gut

questions.why: The midgut–hindgut boundary.

questions.stem: The marginal artery is formed by anastomoses along the:
questions.why: It links branches of the SMA and IMA.

questions.stem: The left renal vein usually passes:

options.label: A
options.text: behind the aorta, above the coeliac trunk

options.label: B
options.text: in front of the SMA at the L1 level

options.label: C
options.text: behind the IVC near the renal hilum

options.label: D
options.text: in front of the IVC, below the renal artery

options.label: E
options.text: in front of the aorta, below the SMA

questions.why: It can be compressed between the SMA and aorta (nutcracker).

questions.stem: A catheter for pulmonary artery monitoring reaches the right atrium most commonly through the:

options.label: C
options.text: great saphenous or common femoral vein

questions.why: It then passes through the tricuspid valve to the pulmonary trunk.

questions.stem: Portocaval anastomoses are clinically important because in portal hypertension they:

options.label: C
options.text: divert blood into the pulmonary veins

options.label: D
options.text: raise pressure in the coronary sinus

questions.why: E.g. oesophageal varices and haemorrhoids.

questions.stem: Continuous capillaries are typical of all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.why: The kidney, gut and endocrine glands have fenestrated capillaries.

questions.stem: Fenestrated capillaries are characteristic of the:
questions.why: Kidneys, intestines and endocrine glands.

questions.stem: The blood–brain barrier depends on brain capillaries that:
questions.why: They are continuous capillaries with no intercellular channels.

questions.stem: Red cells pass through capillaries in single file because the capillary diameter is about:
questions.why: A red cell is about 6–8 µm across.

notes.D: Too narrow for a red cell.

questions.stem: The deep veins that accompany limb arteries in pairs are called:
questions.why: The limbs have superficial and deep (comitant) veins.

questions.stem: The pulse felt just in front of the tragus of the ear is from the:
questions.why: A clinically palpable artery.

notes.B: At the mandible, in front of masseter.

questions.stem: The dorsalis pedis pulse is felt:

options.label: A
options.text: behind the medial malleolus at the ankle

options.label: B
options.text: deep in the roof of the popliteal fossa

options.label: C
options.text: at the midinguinal point below the ligament

options.label: D
options.text: on the dorsum of the foot, lateral to EHL

options.label: E
options.text: below and behind the lateral malleolus

questions.why: The posterior tibial is behind the medial malleolus.

questions.stem: A "bovine arch" of the aorta is one in which:

options.label: A
options.text: the arch passes to the right of the trachea

options.label: B
options.text: the left vertebral artery arises from the arch

options.label: C
options.text: the right subclavian arises last from the arch

options.label: D
options.text: the left subclavian arises from the brachiocephalic

options.label: E
options.text: brachiocephalic and left carotid share an origin

questions.why: The commonest arch variant.

questions.stem: In the fetus, blood bypasses the lungs from the pulmonary trunk to the aorta through the:
questions.why: It becomes the ligamentum arteriosum; failure to close is PDA.

questions.stem: The fetal ductus venosus allows blood to bypass the:
questions.why: It joins the umbilical vein to the IVC.

questions.stem: The left pulmonary artery lies in front of the:

options.label: B
options.text: arch of the aorta and the thymus

questions.why: It is joined to the arch by the ligamentum arteriosum.

notes.C: It lies below the arch; thymus is in front.
notes.E: The right PA passes behind these.

questions.stem: The right renal artery passes:
questions.why: The left renal vein crosses in front of the aorta.

notes.D: Ureter is in front of it.

questions.stem: The SMA crosses anterior to which part of the duodenum?
questions.why: It also lies in front of the uncinate process and left renal vein.

questions.stem: The inferior phrenic arteries supply the diaphragm and the:
questions.why: The left gastric also supplies the adjacent oesophagus.

questions.stem: The gallbladder and duodenum are supplied through branches of the:
questions.why: Liver, stomach, gallbladder, duodenum and pancreas.

questions.stem: Which is a paired (lateral) branch of the abdominal aorta?
questions.why: Paired: inferior phrenic, middle suprarenal, renal, gonadal, lumbar, common iliac.

questions.stem: The inferior mesenteric artery arises at the level of:
questions.why: It supplies the hindgut.

questions.stem: The appendicular artery usually arises from the:
questions.why: A terminal SMA branch.

questions.stem: The short gastric arteries arise from the:
questions.why: They supply the fundus of the stomach.

questions.stem: Caput medusae in portal hypertension results from the portocaval anastomosis at the:
questions.why: Four sites: oesophageal, paraumbilical, rectal, retroperitoneal.

questions.stem: Which is NOT one of the four sites of portocaval anastomosis?
questions.why: The portocaval anastomoses are at the lower oesophagus, anal canal, paraumbilical region and retroperitoneum; the pulmonary hilum has no portal-systemic connection.

questions.stem: If the IVC is blocked below the renal veins, blood can return to the heart mainly through the:

options.label: A
options.text: pulmonary veins to the left atrium

questions.why: Collateral routes link the IVC and SVC systems.

questions.stem: The left gonadal vein usually drains into the:
questions.why: The right gonadal vein enters the IVC directly.

notes.D: Also drains to the left renal.

questions.stem: The brachiocephalic vein is formed by the union of the:
questions.why: The two brachiocephalic veins form the SVC.

questions.stem: Which artery is a branch of the internal carotid?
questions.why: The others branch from the external carotid.

questions.stem: The vertebral artery arises from the:
questions.why: The two vertebrals unite to form the basilar artery.

questions.stem: The ascending aorta lies with the SVC on its right and the:
questions.why: Both lie within the pericardium.

questions.stem: The three circulatory systems are the pulmonary, the systemic (caval) and the:
questions.why: The three circulations are the pulmonary, the systemic (caval) and the portal; the portal system passes through a second (hepatic) capillary bed before returning blood to the heart.

notes.B: Not one of the three as taught.

questions.stem: The tunica media of arteries and veins is composed mainly of:
questions.why: Veins have much less of it than arteries.

questions.stem: The tunica intima consists of the endothelium and:

options.label: A
options.text: a thick layer of circular smooth muscle

options.label: B
options.text: an elastic lamina in collagenous tissue

options.label: C
options.text: a layer of loose fatty tissue

questions.why: The endothelium is simple squamous epithelium lining all vessels.

questions.stem: In the vascular lecture, an arteriovenous shunt is also called a:
questions.why: Blood passes from arteriole to venule directly.

questions.stem: In continuous capillaries, adjacent endothelial cells are:

options.label: A
options.text: widely separated, with large open gaps

options.label: B
options.text: loosely joined, with many large pores

questions.why: CNS capillaries are the exception: they lack the channels.

questions.stem: According to the vascular lecture, sinusoids are found in the liver, bone marrow, spleen and:
questions.why: Discontinuous sinusoidal capillaries occur in the liver, spleen, bone marrow and the adrenal medulla, where wide fenestrations let cells and large molecules pass.

questions.stem: Venous valves, which prevent reflux, are common in veins of the:
questions.why: Valves are numerous in the veins of the limbs (and are also found in the neck), opposing gravity to aid venous return; they are sparse or absent in the great central veins and viscera.

notes.C: Portal system has few or none.

questions.stem: Which is NOT on the list of palpable arteries used clinically?
questions.why: Listed: temporal, carotid, facial, brachial, radial, femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, dorsalis pedis.

questions.stem: Anastomoses between arteries are valuable because, if one artery is blocked, they:

options.label: D
options.text: reduce the oxygen needs of tissue

options.label: E
options.text: convert the artery into a vein

questions.why: End arteries have no such protection.

questions.stem: The ascending aorta ends, and the arch begins, at the level of the:
questions.why: It begins at the left 3rd costal cartilage.

questions.stem: The branches of the aortic arch, in order from right to left, are the:

options.label: A
options.text: right subclavian, right common carotid, left subclavian

options.label: D
options.text: right carotid, left carotid, left subclavian

options.label: E
options.text: brachiocephalic, left common carotid, left subclavian

questions.why: The right common carotid and right subclavian come from the brachiocephalic trunk.

notes.E: Right carotid is not a direct branch.

questions.stem: The right subclavian artery normally arises from the:
questions.why: Arising last from the arch is a variant (aberrant right subclavian).

questions.stem: The pulmonary trunk arises from the:

options.label: A
options.text: aortic vestibule of the left ventricle

questions.why: It divides under the concavity of the aortic arch.

questions.stem: Failure of the ductus arteriosus to close after birth is called:
questions.why: It joins the pulmonary artery to the aorta.

questions.stem: In the fetal heart, the crista dividens directs blood from the IVC through the:
questions.why: It is the lower edge of the septum secundum.

questions.stem: The thoracic aorta becomes the abdominal aorta by passing behind the:
questions.why: At T12.

questions.stem: The subcostal arteries arise from the thoracic aorta at the level of:
questions.why: Posterior intercostals supply spaces 3–11.

questions.stem: Which is a paired branch of the thoracic aorta?
questions.why: Paired: intercostal and superior phrenic. Unpaired (visceral): bronchial, pericardial, oesophageal, mediastinal.

questions.stem: The ventral branches of the abdominal aorta are the coeliac trunk, SMA, IMA and:
questions.why: The others listed are lateral (paired) branches.

questions.stem: Which artery is noted as having no branches before it divides?
questions.why: It ends as the internal and external iliac arteries.

questions.stem: The left gastric artery supplies the stomach and the:
questions.why: The left gastric artery runs along the lesser curvature of the stomach and gives oesophageal branches to the lower oesophagus.

questions.stem: The splenic artery supplies the spleen, stomach and:
questions.why: The splenic artery supplies the spleen, the fundus and greater curvature of the stomach (short gastric and left gastro-omental branches) and the body and tail of the pancreas.

questions.stem: The midgut supplied by the SMA begins at the:
questions.why: It ends two-thirds of the way along the transverse colon.

questions.stem: The SMA lies anterior to the left renal vein, the third part of the duodenum and the:
questions.why: The neck of the pancreas lies in front of it.

notes.E: In front of it, behind the pancreas.

questions.stem: The lowest point of the gut supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery is the:
questions.why: That is the upper third of the anal canal.

notes.C: Below the pectinate line: internal pudendal.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a branch of the inferior mesenteric artery?
questions.why: The right colic is a branch of the SMA.

questions.stem: Which is a branch of the external carotid artery?
questions.why: Also superior thyroid, facial, occipital, posterior auricular, maxillary, superficial temporal.

questions.stem: The basilar artery is formed by the union of the two:
questions.why: It gives pontine and cerebellar branches.

questions.stem: The right suprarenal vein drains into the:
questions.why: The left suprarenal vein drains into the left renal vein.

questions.stem: The azygos vein ends by joining the:
questions.why: It links the caval systems and receives the hemiazygos veins.

questions.stem: The carotid sinus lies at the:

options.label: B
options.text: end of the external carotid artery

options.label: E
options.text: start of the internal carotid artery

questions.why: It is a baroreceptor site.

questions.stem: About compact organs:

options.label: B
options.text: Their stroma encloses and supports the parenchyma

options.label: C
options.text: Trabeculae or septa from the capsule divide them into compartments

options.label: D
options.text: Their blood vessels usually enter at a hilum

notes.E: It may be complete OR incomplete.

questions.why: False: E. It may be complete OR incomplete.

questions.stem: The parenchyma of compact organs is arranged in all of the following patterns EXCEPT:
questions.why: Concentric coats around a cavity describe tubular organs.

questions.stem: Tubular (hollow) organs:

options.label: A
options.text: include segments of the digestive, respiratory and genitourinary tracts

options.label: B
options.text: include blood and lymphatic vascular channels

options.label: C
options.text: have epithelium immediately surrounding the central cavity

options.label: D
options.text: are usually made of three coats: mucosa, muscularis and adventitia or serosa

options.label: E
options.text: have the same number of coats and layers whatever their function

notes.E: FUNCTION determines the number of coats and layers.

questions.why: False: E. FUNCTION determines the number of coats and layers.

questions.stem: A tubular organ lying in a retroperitoneal area is covered externally by:
questions.why: Serosa covers organs within body cavities; adventitia covers retroperitoneal ones.

questions.stem: The system whose tubular organs typically have FOUR coats is the:
questions.why: Mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, serosa/adventitia.

questions.stem: The mediastinum:

options.label: A
options.text: is the interpleural space in and near the midline of the chest

options.label: B
options.text: extends from the sternum to the vertebral column

options.label: C
options.text: contains almost all the thoracic viscera except the lungs

options.label: D
options.text: is divided by a plane from the sternal angle to the lower part of T4

options.label: E
options.text: has the inferior part divided into superior, middle and posterior parts

questions.why: False: E. Inferior = ANTERIOR, middle and posterior.

questions.stem: The superior mediastinum contains:

options.label: A
options.text: the arch of the aorta and its three branches

options.label: B
options.text: the brachiocephalic veins and upper half of the SVC

options.label: D
options.text: the trachea, oesophagus and thoracic duct

questions.why: False: E. That is the middle mediastinum.

questions.stem: Which structure lies in the middle mediastinum?
questions.why: Middle: heart in pericardium, ascending aorta, lower half of SVC, pulmonary trunk and veins, phrenic nerves.

notes.D: Posterior (it only arches into the SVC).

questions.stem: A finger passed behind the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk lies in the:
questions.why: A finger behind the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk, in front of the atria, lies in the transverse pericardial sinus, which separates the arterial from the venous end of the heart.

notes.A: Cul-de-sac behind the left atrium, around the veins.

questions.stem: Accumulation of fluid in the pericardial cavity that compresses the heart is called:
questions.why: Relieved by pericardiocentesis.

notes.C: Right heart failure from lung disease.

questions.stem: The normal apex beat lies in the:

options.label: A
options.text: 4th left intercostal space at the sternal border

options.label: B
options.text: 5th left intercostal space, 8–9 cm from the midline

options.label: C
options.text: 6th left intercostal space at the anterior axillary line

options.label: D
options.text: 5th right intercostal space near the sternum

options.label: E
options.text: 2nd left intercostal space near the sternum

questions.why: About 8–9 cm from the midsternal line, below the nipple in males.

questions.stem: Trabeculae carneae whose apices give rise to the chordae tendineae are the:
questions.why: The papillary muscles are the conical projections of ventricular trabeculae carneae whose apices anchor the chordae tendineae to the atrioventricular valve cusps.

notes.A: A specific band, not this variety.

questions.stem: The mitral area of auscultation lies at the:

options.label: A
options.text: right 2nd intercostal space near the sternum

options.label: B
options.text: left 2nd intercostal space near the sternum

options.label: C
options.text: right 5th intercostal space at the sternum

options.label: D
options.text: left 5th intercostal space at the MCL

options.label: E
options.text: left 4th costal cartilage at the sternum

questions.why: The anatomical mitral valve lies opposite the left 4th costal cartilage, but it is heard best at the apex.

notes.E: Anatomical position, not the auscultation area.

questions.stem: Which is a branch of the left coronary artery?
questions.why: LCA: circumflex, obtuse marginal, anterior interventricular, diagonal, and the SA nodal in 40%.

notes.E: Usually RCA; from the circumflex in about 10%.

questions.stem: The connective tissue framework that supports the parenchyma of a compact organ is the:
questions.why: The capsule and trabeculae form the stroma.

questions.stem: The innermost coat of a tubular organ consists of:
questions.why: The mucosa.

questions.stem: The plane dividing the superior from the inferior mediastinum passes from the sternal angle to the:
questions.why: The transverse thoracic plane.

questions.stem: The thymus remnant in an adult lies in the:
questions.why: With extension into the anterior mediastinum.

questions.stem: The lower half of the superior vena cava lies in the:
questions.why: The upper half is in the superior mediastinum.

questions.stem: The thoracic duct lies in the posterior mediastinum between the:
questions.why: It ascends behind the oesophagus.

questions.stem: The fibrous pericardium is firmly attached inferiorly to the:

options.label: D
options.text: left and right crura of the diaphragm

questions.why: Superiorly it fuses with the great vessels.

questions.stem: The phrenic nerves descend on the pericardium:

options.label: A
options.text: on its posterior surface, behind both lung roots

options.label: C
options.text: on its lateral surfaces, in front of the lung roots

options.label: E
options.text: on the posterior surface of the oesophagus

questions.why: With the pericardiacophrenic vessels.

questions.stem: The oblique sinus of the pericardium lies behind the:
questions.why: A cul-de-sac bounded by reflections around the pulmonary veins and IVC.

questions.stem: Pain from the pericardium is carried mainly by the:
questions.why: Fibrous and parietal serous layers; the visceral layer is insensitive.

questions.stem: Pericardiocentesis is performed to relieve:
questions.why: Fluid is drained from the pericardial cavity.

questions.stem: The base (posterior surface) of the heart is formed mainly by the:
questions.why: It receives the four pulmonary veins.

questions.stem: The right border of the heart is formed by the:
questions.why: Entirely right atrium.

questions.stem: The left auricle appears on the heart's:
questions.why: It overlaps the root of the pulmonary trunk.

questions.stem: The conus arteriosus (infundibulum) differs from the rest of the right ventricle in having:
questions.why: It leads to the pulmonary trunk.

questions.stem: The crista terminalis separates the right atrium into:

options.label: B
options.text: inflow and outflow tracts of the ventricle

questions.why: Marked outside by the sulcus terminalis.

questions.stem: The fossa ovalis is a remnant of the:
questions.why: Its rim is the limbus fossae ovalis.

questions.stem: The AV nodal artery usually arises from the:
questions.why: At the crux, near the posterior interventricular branch.

questions.stem: The great cardiac vein runs with the:
questions.why: It drains into the coronary sinus.

questions.stem: The second heart sound is produced by closure of the:
questions.why: The first sound is closure of the AV valves.

questions.stem: The thyroid gland is the example used for parenchyma arranged as:
questions.why: Thyroid follicles store colloid.

questions.stem: The kidney is the example used for compact-organ parenchyma arranged as:
questions.why: Nephron tubules make up most of the parenchyma.

notes.E: Not one of the listed patterns.

questions.stem: In a tubular organ, the vessels and nerves mainly run in the:

options.label: E
options.text: smooth muscle cells of the muscularis

questions.why: The wall alternates muscle and connective tissue layers.

notes.E: Vessels run between, not within, the muscle cells.

questions.stem: Which function of the cardiovascular system is classed as "protection"?

options.label: A
options.text: Carrying hormones to their target organs

options.label: B
options.text: Carrying oxygen and carbon dioxide gases

options.label: D
options.text: Carrying white cells and clotting factors

questions.why: Regulation is via hormones; transport covers gases, nutrients and waste.

questions.stem: The circulatory system is made up of the:

options.label: A
options.text: heart and the arterial tree only

options.label: C
options.text: heart, lungs and the circulating blood

options.label: D
options.text: lymph nodes, spleen and the thymus

questions.why: Lymph returns tissue fluid to venous blood, filtered by lymph nodes.

questions.stem: Lymph nodes are placed along lymphatic pathways mainly to:

options.label: A

questions.stem: The pharynx communicates anteriorly with all of the following cavities EXCEPT the:
questions.why: The pharynx opens anteriorly into the nasal, oral and laryngeal cavities, not the pericardial cavity.

questions.stem: The superior boundary of the abdominal cavity is formed by the:
questions.why: The diaphragm forms the domed superior boundary of the abdominal cavity.

questions.stem: Inferiorly, the abdominal cavity has no distinct boundary because it is continuous with the pelvic cavity at the:
questions.why: There is no floor to the abdomen proper; it is continuous with the pelvis at the pelvic brim.

questions.stem: The four abdominal quadrants are produced by the intersection of the median plane and the:
questions.why: Median (vertical) and transumbilical (horizontal) planes divide the abdomen into four quadrants.

questions.stem: The transpyloric plane lies at the level of which vertebra?
questions.why: The transpyloric plane of Addison passes at the level of the L1 vertebral body.

questions.stem: The subcostal plane, used to define the nine regions, passes at the level of which vertebra?
questions.why: The subcostal plane joins the lowest points of the costal margin (10th costal cartilage) at L3.

questions.stem: The transtubercular (intertubercular) plane passes at the level of which vertebra?
questions.why: The transtubercular plane joins the iliac tubercles at the L5 level.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the nine abdominal regions?
questions.why: The nine regions include hypochondrium, lumbar, inguinal (groin), epigastric, umbilical and hypogastric; 'suprapubic quadrant' is not a named region.

questions.stem: McBurney's point, used in the diagnosis of appendicitis, lies one-third of the way along a line from the umbilicus to the:

options.label: A
options.text: the crest of the iliac bone

questions.why: McBurney's point is one-third along the line from the right ASIS to the umbilicus.

questions.stem: The linea semilunaris corresponds to the:

options.label: B
options.text: lower free border of external oblique

questions.why: The linea semilunaris is the curved line at the lateral edge of the rectus sheath/rectus abdominis.

questions.stem: The midline fibrous band between the two rectus abdominis muscles, attached from xiphoid process to pubic symphysis, is the:
questions.why: The linea alba is formed by midline fusion of the rectus sheath layers.

questions.stem: Below the umbilicus the superficial fascia splits into a superficial fatty layer and a deep membranous layer; the fatty layer is called:
questions.why: Camper's fascia is the fatty superficial layer; Scarpa's is the deeper membranous layer.

questions.stem: The membranous layer of superficial fascia (Scarpa's fascia) continues into the perineum as:
questions.why: Scarpa's fascia continues into the perineum as Colles' fascia (and over the penis as the superficial penile fascia).

questions.stem: Over the scrotum, the fatty layer of superficial fascia is replaced by:
questions.why: In the scrotum the fat of Camper's fascia is replaced by the smooth dartos muscle.

questions.stem: A characteristic feature of the anterior abdominal wall compared with the limbs is that it has:
questions.why: There is no deep fascia over the anterior abdominal wall muscles.

questions.stem: The external oblique muscle arises from the outer surfaces of which ribs?
questions.why: External oblique originates from the lower eight (5th-12th) ribs.

questions.stem: The fibres of the external oblique muscle run in which direction?
questions.why: External oblique fibres pass downward and medially ('hands in pockets').

questions.stem: The fibres of the internal oblique muscle are generally directed:
questions.why: Internal oblique fibres run upward and medially, at right angles to the external oblique.

questions.stem: Which muscle of the anterolateral abdominal wall has horizontally running fibres and is the main muscle for compressing the abdominal viscera?
questions.why: Transversus abdominis has transverse fibres and is the chief muscle raising intra-abdominal pressure.

questions.stem: The rectus abdominis muscle arises from the pubic symphysis and crest and inserts on the:

options.label: B
options.text: anterior iliac crest and inguinal ligament

questions.why: Rectus abdominis inserts on the xiphoid process and 5th-7th costal cartilages.

questions.stem: The small triangular muscle that lies within the rectus sheath anterior to the lower rectus abdominis and is absent in about 20% of people is the:
questions.why: Pyramidalis tenses the linea alba and is absent in roughly 20% of people.

questions.stem: The anterolateral abdominal wall muscles are chiefly supplied by the anterior rami of which spinal nerves?
questions.why: The thoracoabdominal nerves T7-T11, subcostal T12 and L1 (iliohypogastric/ilioinguinal) supply the wall.

questions.stem: Below the arcuate line, the rectus sheath has:
questions.why: Below the arcuate line all aponeuroses pass in front of rectus, so only an anterior layer remains.

questions.stem: The arcuate line of the rectus sheath is located approximately:

options.label: A
options.text: a little above the pubic symphysis

options.label: B
options.text: just below the anterior costal margin

options.label: C
options.text: a third of the way from umbilicus to pubis

options.label: D
options.text: midway between the xiphoid and umbilicus

options.label: E
options.text: exactly at the level of the umbilicus

questions.why: The arcuate line lies about one-third of the distance from umbilicus to pubic crest.

questions.stem: A defect in which layer is the fundamental basis of an abdominal wall hernia?
questions.why: The transversalis fascia gives the wall its structural integrity; a hernia results from a defect in it.

questions.stem: The external spermatic fascia covering the spermatic cord is derived from the:
questions.why: External spermatic fascia comes from the external oblique aponeurosis.

questions.stem: The cremasteric muscle and fascia of the spermatic cord are derived from the:
questions.why: The cremaster is derived from the internal oblique.

questions.stem: The internal spermatic fascia of the spermatic cord is derived from the:
questions.why: Internal spermatic fascia is a prolongation of the transversalis fascia at the deep ring.

questions.stem: The superior epigastric artery, supplying the upper rectus abdominis, is a continuation of the:
questions.why: Superior epigastric is a terminal branch of the internal thoracic artery.

questions.stem: The inferior epigastric artery arises from the:
questions.why: The inferior epigastric artery is a branch of the external iliac artery, just above the inguinal ligament.

questions.stem: Dilated subcutaneous veins radiating from the umbilicus (caput medusae) result from anastomoses carried by the paraumbilical veins to the:
questions.why: Paraumbilical veins connect the periumbilical network to the portal vein, forming a portal-systemic anastomosis.

questions.stem: The dermatome overlying the umbilicus is supplied by which spinal nerve?
questions.why: The T10 dermatome lies at the level of the umbilicus.

questions.stem: The neurovascular plane of the anterolateral abdominal wall lies between the:

options.label: A
options.text: the rectus abdominis and its own sheath

options.label: C
options.text: the external and the internal oblique layers

options.label: D
options.text: the skin and the external oblique muscle

questions.why: Nerves and vessels run in the plane between internal oblique and transversus abdominis.

questions.stem: The median umbilical fold on the internal surface of the anterior abdominal wall is raised by the:

options.label: A
options.text: remnant of the round ligament of liver

questions.why: The median umbilical fold overlies the urachal remnant (median umbilical ligament).

questions.stem: The lateral umbilical folds are raised by the:
questions.why: The lateral umbilical folds contain the inferior epigastric vessels.

questions.stem: The inguinal ligament is formed by the rolled-under inferior border of the aponeurosis of the:
questions.why: The inguinal ligament (of Poupart) is the folded lower edge of the external oblique aponeurosis.

questions.stem: The inguinal canal is approximately how long in the adult?
questions.why: The inguinal canal is about 4 cm long, running from the deep to the superficial ring.

questions.stem: The deep (internal) inguinal ring is an opening in the:
questions.why: The deep inguinal ring is an evagination of the transversalis fascia.

questions.stem: The deep inguinal ring lies lateral to which vessels?
questions.why: The deep ring lies lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, 1.25 cm above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament.

questions.stem: The superficial (external) inguinal ring is a defect in the:
questions.why: The superficial ring is a triangular defect in the external oblique aponeurosis, above and lateral to the pubic tubercle.

questions.stem: The roof of the inguinal canal is formed by the arching fibres of the:

options.label: A
options.text: the external and the internal oblique muscles

options.label: B
options.text: the transversalis fascia and the peritoneum

options.label: C
options.text: the inguinal and the lacunar ligaments

options.label: D
options.text: the rectus abdominis and the pyramidalis

questions.why: The roof is formed by the arching lowest fibres of internal oblique and transversus abdominis.

questions.stem: The anterior wall of the inguinal canal is formed mainly by the:
questions.why: The anterior wall is the external oblique aponeurosis, reinforced laterally by internal oblique.

questions.stem: The posterior wall of the inguinal canal is formed by the transversalis fascia reinforced medially by the:
questions.why: The posterior wall is transversalis fascia, reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon (falx inguinalis).

questions.stem: Which structure passes through the inguinal canal in BOTH sexes?
questions.why: The ilioinguinal nerve traverses the canal in both sexes; the cord (male) or round ligament (female) is sex-specific.

questions.stem: The conjoint tendon (falx inguinalis) is formed by the lower fibres of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis and inserts on the pubic crest and the:
questions.why: The conjoint tendon inserts on the pubic crest and pectineal line.

questions.stem: The medial boundary of the femoral canal is formed by the:
questions.why: The femoral canal is bounded medially by the lacunar ligament (of Gimbernat).

questions.stem: The lateral boundary of the femoral canal is the:
questions.why: The femoral vein lies immediately lateral to the femoral canal.

questions.stem: The boundaries of Hesselbach's (inguinal) triangle include the inferior epigastric vessels laterally, the inguinal ligament inferiorly, and medially the:

options.label: C
options.text: medial border of the psoas major

questions.why: Hesselbach's triangle is bounded medially by the lateral border of rectus abdominis; direct hernias occur here.

questions.stem: An indirect inguinal hernia enters the inguinal canal through the deep ring, lying which way in relation to the inferior epigastric vessels?
questions.why: An indirect hernia passes lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels through the deep ring.

questions.stem: A direct inguinal hernia bulges through the posterior wall of the inguinal canal, lying which way in relation to the inferior epigastric vessels?
questions.why: A direct hernia pushes through Hesselbach's triangle, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.

questions.stem: A congenital indirect inguinal hernia results from persistence of the:
questions.why: A patent processus vaginalis allows a congenital indirect hernia (and connects to the tunica vaginalis).

questions.stem: Compared with an indirect hernia, the neck of a direct inguinal hernia sac is:

options.label: A
options.text: wide, so less likely to strangulate

options.label: B
options.text: narrow, so more likely to strangulate

questions.why: A direct hernia has a wide neck and is less likely to strangulate; an indirect hernia has a narrow neck.

questions.stem: A femoral hernia, which passes through the femoral canal, is more common in:
questions.why: Femoral hernias are more common in women; the sac lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.

questions.stem: The testis is drawn down into the scrotum during fetal life by the:
questions.why: The gubernaculum guides testicular descent through the inguinal canal into the scrotum.

questions.stem: The quadratus lumborum muscle inserts onto the:

options.label: A
options.text: internal lip of the iliac crest

options.label: C
options.text: tips of the lumbar transverse processes

options.label: D
options.text: body of the twelfth thoracic vertebra

questions.why: QL arises from the lumbar transverse processes and 12th rib and inserts on the internal lip of the iliac crest.

questions.stem: During inspiration the quadratus lumborum assists breathing by:

options.label: A
options.text: expanding the lower costal cartilages outward

options.label: B
options.text: anchoring the 12th rib against the diaphragm

options.label: C
options.text: actively elevating the first and second ribs

options.label: D
options.text: depressing the sternum and the manubrium

options.label: E
options.text: flexing the whole thoracic vertebral column

questions.why: QL fixes the 12th rib so the diaphragm can descend effectively during inspiration.

questions.stem: The psoas major muscle unites with the iliacus to insert, as the iliopsoas, onto the:

options.label: E
options.text: internal lip of the iliac crest

questions.why: Psoas major and iliacus fuse as iliopsoas and insert on the lesser trochanter.

questions.stem: The psoas major muscle is innervated by the anterior rami of which nerves?
questions.why: Psoas major receives direct branches from the ventral rami of L1-L3.

questions.stem: The iliacus muscle is innervated by the:
questions.why: Iliacus is supplied by the femoral nerve (L2-L4), unlike psoas major which gets direct ventral rami.

questions.stem: The psoas minor muscle, absent in about 40% of people, inserts onto the:
questions.why: Psoas minor inserts on the iliopubic eminence and flexes the lumbar vertebral column.

questions.stem: Which posterior abdominal wall muscle is reported to be absent in roughly 40% of people?
questions.why: Psoas minor is the variable muscle, absent in about 40% of individuals.

questions.stem: The right dome of the diaphragm sits higher than the left mainly because of the:
questions.why: The bulk of the liver pushes the right hemidiaphragm higher than the left.

questions.stem: The muscular fibres of the diaphragm converge to insert onto the:
questions.why: The diaphragmatic muscle fibres insert on the trifoliate central tendon.

questions.stem: The motor nerve supply to the diaphragm is the:
questions.why: The phrenic nerve (C3-C5) provides all motor fibres to the diaphragm.

questions.stem: Sensation from the peripheral part of the diaphragm is carried by the:
questions.why: The peripheral diaphragm is supplied by intercostal nerves; the central part is phrenic.

questions.stem: The right crus of the diaphragm arises from the bodies of vertebrae:
questions.why: The longer right crus arises from L1-L3; the left crus from L1-L2.

questions.stem: The medial arcuate ligament of the diaphragm arches over the:
questions.why: The medial arcuate ligament is a thickening over psoas major; the lateral arcuate ligament overlies QL.

questions.stem: The lateral arcuate ligament of the diaphragm arches over the:

options.label: B
options.text: the head of the twelfth rib

options.label: E
options.text: the belly of the psoas major

questions.why: The lateral arcuate ligament overlies quadratus lumborum, running from the TP of L1 to rib 12.

questions.stem: The aortic hiatus of the diaphragm lies at the level of which vertebra?
questions.why: The aortic hiatus is at T12, behind the median arcuate ligament.

questions.stem: In addition to the aorta, the aortic hiatus transmits the:
questions.why: The aortic hiatus transmits the aorta, thoracic duct and azygos vein.

questions.stem: The caval opening of the diaphragm lies at the level of which vertebra?
questions.why: The caval hiatus is at T8, within the central tendon.

questions.stem: The caval opening of the diaphragm is located within the:
questions.why: The IVC passes through the central tendon at T8.

questions.stem: The oesophageal hiatus of the diaphragm lies at the level of which vertebra?
questions.why: The oesophageal hiatus is at T10, in the muscular right crus.

questions.stem: Besides the oesophagus, the oesophageal hiatus transmits the:

options.label: A
options.text: the thoracic duct and azygos vein

options.label: C
options.text: the aorta and the thoracic duct

questions.why: The oesophageal hiatus transmits the vagal trunks and oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels.

questions.stem: The most common type of hiatus hernia is the:
questions.why: The sliding (type I) hiatus hernia is by far the most common.

questions.stem: In a type IV hiatus hernia, the characteristic finding is that the:

options.label: B
options.text: entire stomach lies within the thorax

options.label: E
options.text: defect lies within the central tendon

questions.why: A type IV hernia has the entire stomach (and sometimes other organs) in the thorax.

questions.stem: The lumbar plexus is formed by the anterior rami of nerves and lies within the substance of the:
questions.why: The lumbar plexus (L1-L4) forms within the psoas major.

questions.stem: The lumbar plexus is formed by the anterior rami of which spinal nerves?
questions.why: The lumbar plexus arises from the ventral rami of L1-L4.

questions.stem: The lumbosacral trunk, which joins the sacral plexus, is formed from part of L4 and the whole of:
questions.why: The lumbosacral trunk (L4-L5) links the lumbar and sacral plexuses.

questions.stem: The iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves both arise mainly from which spinal level?
questions.why: Both the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves come principally from L1.

questions.stem: Within the inguinal canal, the ilioinguinal nerve accompanies the:
questions.why: The ilioinguinal nerve runs with the spermatic cord (or round ligament) and exits the superficial ring.

questions.stem: The genitofemoral nerve emerges from and pierces the anterior surface of which muscle?
questions.why: The genitofemoral nerve pierces and runs on the anterior surface of psoas major.

questions.stem: The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve supplies motor fibres to the:
questions.why: The genital branch supplies the cremaster and sensation to the scrotal/labial skin.

questions.stem: The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is derived from which spinal levels?
questions.why: The lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh arises from L2-L3 and supplies anterolateral thigh skin.

questions.stem: The femoral nerve emerges at the lateral border of the psoas major and is formed from which spinal levels?
questions.why: The femoral nerve (L2-L4, posterior divisions) supplies iliacus and the anterior thigh.

questions.stem: The femoral nerve gives rise to a long cutaneous branch that accompanies the great saphenous vein, the:
questions.why: The saphenous nerve is the terminal cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve.

questions.stem: The obturator nerve emerges from which border of the psoas major?
questions.why: The obturator nerve appears at the medial border of psoas major, unlike the femoral at the lateral border.

questions.stem: The obturator nerve provides motor supply mainly to the:
questions.why: The obturator nerve supplies the medial (adductor) compartment of the thigh.

questions.stem: Because the obturator nerve supplies both the hip and knee joints, disease of the hip may produce referred pain in the:
questions.why: The obturator nerve innervates both joints, so hip pathology can refer pain to the knee.

questions.stem: The subcostal nerve that runs on the posterior abdominal wall is the anterior ramus of which nerve?
questions.why: The subcostal nerve is the ventral ramus of T12, running below the 12th rib onto the posterior wall.

questions.stem: The abdominal oesophagus pierces the diaphragm through the right crus at the level of which vertebra?
questions.why: The oesophagus passes through the oesophageal hiatus in the right crus at T10.

questions.stem: The abdominal oesophagus terminates in the cardiac part of the stomach at approximately the level of:
questions.why: The oesophagus ends at the cardia at about T11.

questions.stem: At the lower oesophagus, the anterior and posterior vagal trunks lie respectively on its:
questions.why: The left vagus forms the anterior trunk and the right vagus the posterior trunk on the lower oesophagus.

questions.stem: Which of the following contributes to the lower oesophageal (physiological) sphincter mechanism?

options.label: A
options.text: the left crus gripping the aorta

options.label: C
options.text: tone of the external anal sphincter

options.label: D
options.text: the right crus acting as a pinch-cock

questions.why: The right crus pinches the lower oesophagus; with the acute angle of entry and intra-abdominal pressure it forms the LES.

questions.stem: The widest and most dilated part of the alimentary tract is the:
questions.why: The stomach is the widest part of the gut.

questions.stem: The cardiac orifice of the stomach lies to the left of the midline at the level of:
questions.why: The cardia (gastro-oesophageal junction) lies left of the T10 vertebra.

questions.stem: The pylorus of the stomach lies to the right of the midline at the level of:
questions.why: The pylorus (gastroduodenal junction) lies to the right of the L1 vertebra (transpyloric plane).

questions.stem: The longitudinal mucosal folds seen in the empty stomach are called:
questions.why: Gastric rugae are the longitudinal mucosal folds of the stomach.

questions.stem: The pyloric sphincter is a thickening of which muscle layer of the stomach wall?
questions.why: The pyloric sphincter is formed by thickening of the middle circular muscle layer.

questions.stem: Which structure is part of the posterior relations ('stomach bed') of the stomach?
questions.why: The stomach bed includes the pancreas, splenic artery, left kidney and suprarenal, spleen and transverse mesocolon.

questions.stem: A posterior gastric ulcer eroding backwards may cause torrential haemorrhage by involving the:
questions.why: The splenic artery runs along the stomach bed and may be eroded by a posterior ulcer.

questions.stem: The total length of the duodenum is approximately:
questions.why: The duodenum is about 25 cm (10 inches) long.

questions.stem: The duodenum curves in a C-shape around the head of the:
questions.why: The C-shaped duodenum encloses the head of the pancreas.

questions.stem: Which part of the duodenum is the 'duodenal cap' seen on barium radiographs and is devoid of circular mucosal folds?
questions.why: The first (superior) part is the mobile duodenal cap, lacking circular folds and supplied by end arteries.

questions.stem: The common bile duct and main pancreatic duct open into which part of the duodenum?
questions.why: The hepatopancreatic ampulla opens at the major papilla in the second part of the duodenum.

questions.stem: The third (horizontal) part of the duodenum is crossed anteriorly by the:
questions.why: The superior mesenteric vessels cross the third part; their compression causes SMA (Wilkie) syndrome.

questions.stem: The duodenojejunal flexure is held in position by the suspensory muscle (ligament) of:
questions.why: The suspensory ligament of Treitz fixes the duodenojejunal flexure to the right crus.

questions.stem: Together, the jejunum and ileum measure approximately:
questions.why: The jejunum and ileum together are about 6 m long (jejunum two-fifths, ileum three-fifths).

questions.stem: Compared with the ileum, the jejunum characteristically has:

options.label: D
options.text: fewer arterial arcades and longer vasa recta

options.label: E
options.text: more arterial arcades and shorter vasa recta

questions.why: The jejunum has few arcades with long vasa recta; the ileum has many arcades with short vasa recta.

questions.stem: Aggregated lymphoid follicles (Peyer's patches) are most abundant in the:
questions.why: Peyer's patches are most numerous in the ileum.

questions.stem: Vitamin B12 and conjugated bile acids are maximally absorbed in the:
questions.why: The terminal ileum is the site of maximal absorption of B12 and conjugated bile acids.

questions.stem: A congenital outpouching of the ileum, a remnant of the vitelline duct, is called a:
questions.why: Meckel's (ileal) diverticulum is a persistent portion of the vitelline duct.

questions.stem: The ileum opens into the large intestine at the:
questions.why: The ileum ends at the ileocaecal valve, entering the caecum.

questions.stem: The vermiform appendix is attached to the posteromedial wall of the caecum and is best located by tracing the:
questions.why: The three teniae coli converge at the base of the appendix, guiding the surgeon to it.

questions.stem: Which parts of the colon are retroperitoneal?
questions.why: The ascending and descending colon are retroperitoneal; the transverse and sigmoid have a mesocolon.

questions.stem: The three narrow bands of outer longitudinal muscle on the colon are the:
questions.why: Teniae coli are the three longitudinal muscle bands of the caecum and colon.

questions.stem: The sacculations of the colon produced because the teniae are shorter than the gut are called:
questions.why: Haustra are the pouches produced by the relatively short teniae coli.

questions.stem: The fat-filled peritoneal pouches hanging from the colon are the:

options.label: D
options.text: the haustra of the colon wall

questions.why: Omental (epiploic) appendices are fat-filled tags of visceral peritoneum on the colon.

questions.stem: The rectum begins as a continuation of the sigmoid colon at the level of which sacral vertebra?
questions.why: The rectum begins at S3, following the sacral curve.

questions.stem: Which feature is characteristically ABSENT from the rectum?
questions.why: The rectum has no teniae coli, haustra or omental appendices; the teniae broaden into continuous muscle.

questions.stem: The anal canal is divided into upper and lower parts by the:
questions.why: The pectinate line divides the endodermal upper two-thirds from the ectodermal lower third.

questions.stem: A carcinoma arising ABOVE the pectinate line of the anal canal is typically a(n):
questions.why: The upper (visceral/endodermal) anal canal gives rise to adenocarcinoma; the lower part to squamous carcinoma.

questions.stem: The external anal sphincter is composed of:
questions.why: The external anal sphincter is skeletal muscle; the internal sphincter is smooth muscle.

questions.stem: The largest gland in the human body, weighing on average about 1.5 kg, is the:
questions.why: The liver is the largest gland, about 1.5 kg.

questions.stem: The quadrate lobe of the liver lies between the gallbladder and the:

options.label: D
options.text: the bare area of the liver

questions.why: The quadrate lobe lies between the gallbladder fossa and the fissure for the round ligament.

questions.stem: The caudate lobe of the liver lies between the inferior vena cava and the:
questions.why: The caudate lobe lies between the IVC, the fissure for the ligamentum venosum and the porta hepatis.

questions.stem: The round ligament of the liver (ligamentum teres hepatis) is the fibrous remnant of the:
questions.why: The ligamentum teres is the obliterated left umbilical vein, lying in the free edge of the falciform ligament.

questions.stem: The ligamentum venosum of the liver is the remnant of the:
questions.why: The ligamentum venosum is the fibrous remnant of the fetal ductus venosus.

questions.stem: The porta hepatis transmits the portal triad, which consists of the hepatic portal vein, common bile duct and the:
questions.why: The portal triad at the porta hepatis is the portal vein, proper hepatic artery and common bile duct.

questions.stem: The functional (surgical) division of the liver into right and left halves is marked by:

options.label: B
options.text: the fissure for the round ligament

questions.why: Cantlie's line runs from the IVC to the gallbladder fossa, dividing the liver functionally.

questions.stem: The liver is held in position in the abdomen mainly by the attachment of the:

options.label: A
options.text: hepatic veins to the inferior vena cava

options.label: B
options.text: falciform ligament to the abdominal wall

questions.why: The liver is held chiefly by the hepatic veins draining into the IVC.

questions.stem: Bile leaving the gallbladder passes into the common bile duct through the:
questions.why: Bile leaves the gallbladder via the cystic duct, which joins the common hepatic duct to form the CBD.

questions.stem: The common bile duct and main pancreatic duct unite to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla of:
questions.why: The ducts join at the ampulla of Vater, which opens at the major duodenal papilla.

questions.stem: Contraction of the gallbladder to release bile is stimulated by vagal fibres and the hormone:
questions.why: CCK (with vagal input) contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi.

questions.stem: The cystohepatic triangle of Calot is bounded by the common hepatic duct, the cystic duct and the:
questions.why: Calot's triangle is bounded by the cystic duct, common hepatic duct and cystic artery.

questions.stem: The pancreas is retroperitoneal except for part of its:
questions.why: The tail of the pancreas is the only intraperitoneal part, lying in the splenorenal ligament.

questions.stem: The uncinate process of the pancreas lies posterior to the:
questions.why: The uncinate process projects behind the superior mesenteric artery.

questions.stem: The tail of the pancreas reaches which structure within the splenorenal ligament?
questions.why: The pancreatic tail ends at the splenic hilum and contains the most islets of Langerhans.

questions.stem: The main pancreatic duct is also known as the duct of:
questions.why: The main pancreatic duct is the duct of Wirsung; the accessory duct is that of Santorini.

questions.stem: Insulin is secreted by which cells of the pancreatic islets?
questions.why: Islet beta cells secrete insulin; alpha cells glucagon; delta cells somatostatin.

questions.stem: The spleen normally lies deep to which ribs?
questions.why: The spleen lies in the left hypochondrium beneath ribs 9-11.

questions.stem: The two peritoneal ligaments connected to the hilum of the spleen are the gastrosplenic ligament and the:
questions.why: The gastrosplenic and splenorenal (lienorenal) ligaments attach at the splenic hilum.

questions.stem: The parasympathetic supply to the foregut and midgut of the gastrointestinal tract is carried by the:
questions.why: The vagus supplies foregut and midgut; pelvic splanchnics supply the hindgut.

questions.stem: The parasympathetic supply to the hindgut is provided by the:
questions.why: Pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4) supply the hindgut; the vagus supplies foregut and midgut.

questions.stem: The greater splanchnic nerve (T5-T9) synapses mainly in the:
questions.why: The greater splanchnic nerve synapses in the coeliac ganglion.

questions.stem: Preganglionic sympathetic fibres to the gut synapse in prevertebral (preaortic) ganglia, which include the:

options.label: B
options.text: terminal ganglia in the gut wall

questions.why: Sympathetic preganglionics synapse in the coeliac, superior and inferior mesenteric ganglia.

questions.stem: Preganglionic parasympathetic fibres to the gut synapse in ganglia located:

options.label: B
options.text: within the wall of the gut

questions.why: Parasympathetic preganglionics synapse in terminal (intramural) ganglia within the gut wall.

questions.stem: Referred pain from a foregut structure such as the stomach is typically felt in the:
questions.why: Foregut pain (T5-T9) is referred to the epigastric region.

questions.stem: Referred pain from a midgut structure such as the appendix is initially felt in the:
questions.why: Midgut pain (T10-T11) is referred to the umbilical region before localising.

questions.stem: Referred pain from hindgut structures such as the descending colon is felt in the:
questions.why: Hindgut pain (L1-L2) is referred to the suprapubic (hypogastric) region.

questions.stem: The kidneys normally extend between which vertebral levels?
questions.why: The kidneys lie against the posterior abdominal wall from about T12 to L3.

questions.stem: The long axis of each kidney runs parallel to the lateral border of which muscle?
questions.why: Each kidney lies obliquely with its long axis along the lateral border of psoas major.

questions.stem: Because each kidney lies obliquely on psoas major, its upper pole is

options.label: B
options.text: at the level of the iliac crest

options.label: C
options.text: nearer the midline than the lower pole

options.label: D
options.text: further from the midline than the lower pole

questions.why: The oblique lie brings the upper pole closer to the midline (and more posterior) than the lower pole.

questions.stem: The transpyloric plane passes through the hila such that it crosses the

options.label: D
options.text: superior part of the right hilum and inferior part of the left hilum

options.label: E
options.text: inferior part of the right hilum and superior part of the left hilum

questions.why: The transpyloric plane (L1) crosses the upper right hilum and the lower left hilum.

questions.stem: During quiet respiration the kidneys move within their fascial sheath by about
questions.why: The kidneys descend and ascend 2-3 cm with respiration, moving only up and down.

questions.stem: From the kidney surface outward, the correct order of coverings is

options.label: A
options.text: fibrous capsule, perirenal fat, renal fascia, pararenal fat

options.label: B
options.text: renal fascia, perirenal fat, fibrous capsule, pararenal fat

options.label: C
options.text: perirenal fat, fibrous capsule, pararenal fat, renal fascia

options.label: D
options.text: pararenal fat, renal fascia, perirenal fat, fibrous capsule

options.label: E
options.text: fibrous capsule, renal fascia, perirenal fat, pararenal fat

questions.why: Inside to outside: true fibrous capsule, perirenal fat, renal (Gerota's) fascia, then pararenal fat.

questions.stem: The renal (Gerota's) fascia encloses the kidney, perirenal fat and also the
questions.why: Renal fascia encloses the kidney, perirenal fat, vessels, upper ureter and the suprarenal gland.

questions.stem: Downward tracking of a perinephric abscess toward the pelvis is possible because the renal fascia is
questions.why: The inferior part of the renal fascia has weak or absent attachments, so pus or fluid can track down to the pelvis.

questions.stem: Downward displacement of the kidney by more than about 5 cm is termed
questions.why: Nephroptosis ('floating kidney') is descent >5 cm from poor fascial/fat support and can kink the ureter.

questions.stem: The fat-filled space inside the kidney that houses the pelvis, calyces and vessels is the
questions.why: The renal sinus, entered through the hilum, contains the renal pelvis, calyces, vessels and nerves in fat.

questions.stem: The combined capacity of the renal pelvis and calyces is only about
questions.why: The pelvicalyceal system holds roughly 8 ml, which matters when injecting contrast.

questions.stem: Inward extensions of cortical tissue that lie between the renal pyramids are the
questions.why: Renal columns of Bertin are cortical extensions separating the pyramids.

questions.stem: The apex of a renal pyramid, which projects into a minor calyx, is the
questions.why: The papilla is the pyramid apex; its papillary ducts open into the minor calyx.

questions.stem: At the renal hilum, the structures from superior to inferior are arranged as
questions.why: Superior to inferior the hilar order is artery, vein, pelvis (AVP); front to back it is vein, artery, pelvis (VAP).

questions.stem: An extrarenal (protruding) renal pelvis, compared with an intrarenal one, makes
questions.why: A pelvis that protrudes outside the parenchyma is easier to open surgically for stones than a buried (intrarenal) pelvis.

questions.stem: The renal artery arises from the abdominal aorta at about the level of

options.label: A
options.text: L2, just below the superior mesenteric artery

options.label: E
options.text: L3, at the inferior mesenteric artery

questions.why: The renal arteries leave the aorta at L2, just below the superior mesenteric artery.

questions.stem: The kidneys receive approximately what fraction of the resting cardiac output?
questions.why: The kidneys take about 20-25% of resting cardiac output.

questions.stem: The left renal vein is longer than the right and is preferred for live-donor nephrectomy; it crosses the midline
questions.why: The left renal vein passes anterior to the aorta (and behind the SMA) and is about three times longer than the right.

questions.stem: The left renal vein, unlike the right, receives the
questions.why: The left renal vein receives the left suprarenal, gonadal and a lumbar vein; the right gonadal and suprarenal veins drain directly to the IVC.

questions.stem: Compression of the left renal vein between the aorta and the superior mesenteric artery causes
questions.why: Nutcracker syndrome is left-renal-vein compression, giving haematuria, flank pain and sometimes a left varicocele.

questions.stem: The relatively avascular surgical plane of the kidney, used for incisions during nephrolithotomy, is the
questions.why: The avascular line of Brodel lies between the anterior and posterior arterial territories, on the posterolateral border.

questions.stem: An inferior polar (accessory) renal artery is clinically important because it may
questions.why: A lower polar artery can cross the pelviureteric junction and obstruct it, producing hydronephrosis.

questions.stem: Lymph from the kidney drains directly to the
questions.why: Renal lymph drains to the para-aortic (lateral aortic) nodes at L2.

questions.stem: Sympathetic fibres to the kidney synapse mainly in the
questions.why: Renal sympathetics (T10-L1) relay chiefly in the aorticorenal ganglion and form the renal plexus.

questions.stem: Stimulation of the renal sympathetic nerves produces
questions.why: Sympathetic activity causes renal vasoconstriction, lowers GFR and stimulates renin release.

questions.stem: Renal pain from capsular stretch or pelviureteric obstruction is typically felt in the
questions.why: Renal pain is referred to the flank/loin in the T12-L1 distribution and may radiate to the groin.

questions.stem: Tenderness elicited by percussion at the costovertebral angle (Murphy's kidney punch) suggests
questions.why: Costovertebral-angle tenderness points to renal inflammation such as acute pyelonephritis.

questions.stem: The right suprarenal gland is pyramidal in shape, while the left is
questions.why: The right adrenal is pyramidal; the left is crescentic (semilunar).

questions.stem: The suprarenal gland is separated from the upper pole of the kidney by
questions.why: Although both lie within the renal fascia, perirenal fat separates the suprarenal gland from the kidney.

questions.stem: The three arteries supplying each suprarenal gland arise from the inferior phrenic artery, the aorta and the
questions.why: Superior suprarenal (from inferior phrenic), middle (from aorta) and inferior (from renal artery) supply the gland.

questions.stem: The right suprarenal vein drains into the IVC, whereas the left suprarenal vein drains into the
questions.why: The short right suprarenal vein enters the IVC; the left drains into the left renal vein.

questions.stem: The suprarenal medulla is innervated by

options.label: E
options.text: somatic fibres of the pudendal nerve

questions.why: Preganglionic sympathetic fibres (greater splanchnic, via the coeliac plexus) synapse directly on medullary chromaffin cells; the medulla has no parasympathetic supply.

questions.stem: The ureter is approximately how long?
questions.why: The ureter is a 25-30 cm retroperitoneal fibromuscular tube.

questions.stem: At operation a ureter is identified because, when gently pinched, it
questions.why: A ureter is whitish, non-pulsatile and shows peristalsis when pinched (Kelly's sign).

questions.stem: The fibromuscular sheath that fixes the pelvic ureter to the bladder is the
questions.why: The pelvic ureter is enveloped by Waldeyer's sheath, anchoring it to the bladder.

questions.stem: The oblique passage of the intravesical ureter through the bladder wall functions to
questions.why: The oblique intramural course acts as a flap valve, preventing reflux when the bladder contracts.

questions.stem: The three normal constrictions of the ureter are the pelviureteric junction, the pelvic brim, and the
questions.why: The ureterovesical junction, where the ureter pierces the bladder, is the narrowest of the three constrictions.

questions.stem: At the pelvic brim the ureter is constricted as it crosses the
questions.why: The ureter is narrowed where it crosses the common iliac artery bifurcation at the pelvic brim.

questions.stem: In the male pelvis, the ureter near its termination is crossed superficially by the
questions.why: The vas deferens crosses superficial (anterior) to the ureter in the male pelvis.

questions.stem: In the female, the structure that crosses anterior to the ureter near the lateral fornix ('water under the bridge') is the
questions.why: The uterine artery crosses above (anterior to) the ureter near the lateral vaginal fornix - 'water under the bridge'.

questions.stem: Ureteric peristalsis is generated primarily by

options.label: A
options.text: pacemaker cells in the renal pelvis

questions.why: Pacemaker cells in the renal pelvis/minor calyces drive peristalsis; autonomic input is only modulatory.

questions.stem: Ureteric colic from a stone classically radiates
questions.why: Ureteric colic (T11-L2 afferents) refers pain from the loin to the groin, scrotum/labia or tip of penis.

questions.stem: During dissection, the abdominal ureter's blood supply is approached from the lateral side because its vessels there arise
questions.why: Abdominal ureteric vessels come from medial sources, so dissection is kept lateral; in the pelvis vessels are lateral, so dissection is medial.

questions.stem: The smooth muscle that forms the wall of the bladder and contracts during micturition is the
questions.why: The detrusor is the bladder-wall smooth muscle that contracts to expel urine.

questions.stem: In young children, before it is purely pelvic, the bladder is
questions.why: In children the bladder lies in the abdomen; it becomes a pelvic organ in the adult (except when very full).

questions.stem: The normal adult bladder capacity is about
questions.why: The adult bladder comfortably holds about 400-600 ml.

questions.stem: The trigone of the bladder is bounded by the two ureteric orifices and the
questions.why: The trigone is the smooth triangle between the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice.

questions.stem: Unlike the rest of the bladder lining, the trigone is
questions.why: The trigone mucosa is smooth and firmly bound down, lacking the rugae of the rest of the bladder.

questions.stem: The ridge between the two ureteric orifices that guides the cystoscopist to them is the
questions.why: The interureteric bar (bar of Mercier) connects the ureteric orifices and guides cystoscopy.

questions.stem: The uvula vesicae, a mucosal elevation behind the internal urethral orifice, is produced by the
questions.why: The uvula vesicae overlies the prostatic median lobe, which is prone to benign hyperplasia.

questions.stem: The retropubic space between the bladder and pubic symphysis is the
questions.why: The retropubic space (of Retzius) separates the anterior bladder from the pubic symphysis.

questions.stem: The apex of the bladder is attached to the umbilicus by the median umbilical ligament, a remnant of the
questions.why: The median umbilical ligament is the fibrous remnant of the urachus (allantois).

questions.stem: In the male, the base (posterior surface) of the bladder is related to the
questions.why: The male bladder base relates to the seminal vesicles and the ampullae of the vasa deferentia.

questions.stem: The male bladder base is separated from the rectum by
questions.why: Denonvilliers' (rectovesical) fascia lies between the male bladder base/prostate and the rectum.

questions.stem: The bladder is supplied mainly by the superior and inferior vesical arteries, which are branches of the
questions.why: The vesical arteries arise from the internal iliac artery; in females the inferior vesical is replaced by the vaginal artery.

questions.stem: Parasympathetic fibres (S2-S4) to the bladder, on stimulation,

options.label: A
options.text: contract the detrusor, relax the internal sphincter

options.label: B
options.text: relax the detrusor and contract the internal sphincter

options.label: C
options.text: contract both detrusor and internal sphincter

options.label: D
options.text: have no effect on the detrusor

options.label: E
options.text: act only on the external sphincter

questions.why: Pelvic splanchnic (S2-S4) parasympathetic activity empties the bladder: detrusor contraction with internal-sphincter relaxation.

questions.stem: Sympathetic fibres via the hypogastric plexus promote bladder filling by

options.label: B
options.text: relaxing the detrusor and contracting the internal sphincter

options.label: E
options.text: contracting the detrusor and relaxing the internal sphincter

questions.why: Sympathetic activity relaxes the detrusor and contracts the internal urethral sphincter, favouring storage.

questions.stem: The internal urethral sphincter in the male serves the additional function of
questions.why: The male internal sphincter (smooth muscle, sympathetic T11-L2) also prevents retrograde ejaculation.

questions.stem: The external urethral sphincter is skeletal muscle supplied by the
questions.why: The voluntary external sphincter in the urogenital diaphragm is innervated by the pudendal nerve (S2-S4).

questions.stem: The female urethra is short (3-4 cm), which clinically means
questions.why: The short female urethra predisposes to ascending UTI and is easy to catheterize.

questions.stem: The female urethra opens into the vestibule
questions.why: The external urethral orifice lies in the vestibule, anterior to the vaginal opening and behind the clitoris.

questions.stem: The paraurethral (Skene's) glands of the female urethra are the developmental homologue of the
questions.why: Skene's (paraurethral) glands are the female homologue of the prostate.

questions.stem: The longest and widest, most dilatable part of the male urethra is the
questions.why: The prostatic urethra (~3 cm) is the widest and most dilatable part, receiving the prostatic and ejaculatory ducts.

questions.stem: The narrowest and least dilatable part of the male urethra, most liable to rupture during catheterization, is the
questions.why: The membranous urethra (~2 cm), passing through the urogenital diaphragm, is the narrowest and least dilatable.

questions.stem: The spongy (penile) urethra receives the ducts of which glands?
questions.why: The bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands open into the spongy urethra; the ejaculatory and prostatic ducts open into the prostatic urethra.

questions.stem: The prostatic utricle, opening on the seminal colliculus, is a remnant of the
questions.why: The prostatic utricle is the male remnant of the fused paramesonephric ducts (homologue of uterus/vagina).

questions.stem: The spongy urethra drains lymph mainly to the
questions.why: The spongy (penile) urethra drains to the inguinal nodes; the prostatic and membranous parts drain to internal iliac nodes.

questions.stem: Physiological urinary incontinence in infants occurs because
questions.why: Voluntary sphincter control awaits myelination of the corticospinal tracts, developing by about 3-6 years.

questions.stem: Most urinary tract stones (about 75%) are composed of
questions.why: About 75% of stones are calcium oxalate/phosphate; struvite (~15%) and uric acid/cystine (~10%) are less common.

questions.stem: Disintegration of a urinary stone using focused external shock waves is called
questions.why: Extracorporeal shock-wave lithotripsy fragments stones without open surgery.

questions.stem: A transplanted kidney is usually placed in the
questions.why: Renal transplants are placed in the iliac fossa, with anastomosis to the iliac vessels and bladder.

questions.stem: A congenital fusion of the lower poles of both kidneys, trapped under the inferior mesenteric artery, is a
questions.why: A horseshoe kidney is caught beneath the inferior mesenteric artery during ascent and remains low.

questions.stem: The olfactory nerve fibres (CN I) reach the olfactory bulb by passing through the
questions.why: CN I fibres pass through the perforations of the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone.

questions.stem: The optic canal transmits the optic nerve together with the
questions.why: The optic canal carries CN II and the ophthalmic artery.
